title: A sugar and salt reformulation tax
headline: A sugar and salt reformulation tax: RF’s £3.5bn, net of the soft drinks levy.
description: The National Food Strategy’s design, taken up by the Resolution Foundation: £4 a kilogram on sugar and £8 a kilogram on salt sold for use in processed food, charged to manufacturers, replacing the Soft Drinks Industry Levy. RF puts the yield at around £3.5 billion by 2029-30 net of abolishing the levy. The point of the tax is to change recipes, so a yield that holds is a sign it has not worked; the figure is held flat in cash here.

baselinePolicy.text: The Soft Drinks Industry Levy charges 18p or 24p a litre on sugary drinks; there is no tax on sugar or salt in other food. The government has consulted on extending the levy to milk-based drinks.

source.quote: An expected slight broadening of the SDIL will not raise as much money as that

alreadyIncludes: The Soft Drinks Industry Levy at its current rates and scope.

terms.label: The Resolution Foundation’s yield for a Sugar and Salt Reformulation Tax at £4/kg and £8/kg, net of the soft drinks levy
terms.unit: £ million, 2029-30, net of abolishing the Soft Drinks Industry Levy

source.quote: this would raise around £3.5 billion by 2029-30 – net of abolishing the SDIL

rawSource.note: RF’s 2029-30 figure held flat in cash from the start year. It is net of the soft drinks levy it replaces.

caveats: A think-tank figure on the National Food Strategy’s design; nobody in government has costed it. Net of the soft drinks levy, which it would replace.
Meant to shrink: the tax is designed to make manufacturers cut sugar and salt, so RF’s yield falls over time if it works. Held flat here.
Regressive in cash: a tax on everyday processed food takes a larger share of a poorer household’s spending, which RF weighs against the health case.

considerations.text: The soft drinks levy cut sugar in drinks sharply before it raised much money; the same response here is the policy’s purpose and would erode the yield.
Charged to manufacturers and passed into food prices; every household pays a little, poorer households a larger share of their budgets, at a time RF says food-price inflation is a live concern.

sources.quote: It is right to be concerned about recent food-price inflation and living standards
